draft.title: The International Date Line
card: The International Date Line is an imaginary line that runs through the Pacific Ocean, close to 180° longitude. It bends in places so that it goes around some countries and islands.
Crossing the line changes the calendar date by one day. The date is not changed by the distance travelled or the time of day.
Going west across the line adds a day. For example, 5 March becomes 6 March.
Going east across the line takes a day away. For example, 5 March becomes 4 March.
draft.remember: West adds a day. East takes a day away.

a.q: A ship sails west across the International Date Line. Just before it crosses, the date is 5 March. What is the date just after?
a.why: Going west across the line adds a day, so 5 March becomes 6 March. Going east would take a day away and give 4 March, which is the tempting mistake of mixing up the directions.
a.clue: Which way is the ship going: does west add or take away?

b.q: Leila sails her yacht east across the International Date Line in the Pacific. Just before she crosses, the date is 1 April. What is the date just after?
b.why: Going east takes a day away, so the date goes back one day from 1 April to 31 March, as March has 31 days. 2 April comes from adding a day, which is what happens going west.
b.clue: East takes a day away, so check the month before April.

problems.detail: The clue states the rule ('East takes a day away') and points to the month before April, so it nearly hands over 31 March. Students no longer have to recall the direction rule.
Question a repeats the card's own example word for word (west, 5 March becomes 6 March), so students can match it from memory without applying the rule. It is very easy for Year 11.

check.summary: The facts and answers are correct (a: 6 March, b: 31 March). However, question b's clue states the rule and points to March, giving the answer away, and question a copies the card's example exactly, making it too easy.

proposal.title: The International Date Line
card: The International Date Line is an imaginary line that runs through the Pacific Ocean, close to 180° longitude. It bends in places so that it goes around some countries and islands.
Crossing the line changes the calendar date by one day. The date is not changed by the distance travelled or the time of day.
Going west across the line adds a day, so the date moves forward one day. For example, 5 March becomes 6 March.
Going east across the line takes a day away, so the date moves back one day. For example, 5 March becomes 4 March.
proposal.remember: West adds a day. East takes a day away.

a.q: A cargo ship sails west across the International Date Line. Just before it crosses, it is Tuesday. What day is it just after?
a.why: Going west across the line adds a day, so Tuesday moves forward to Wednesday. Monday is the tempting mistake: it comes from taking a day away, which is what happens going east.
a.clue: Does the ship's direction move the calendar forward or back?

b.q: Leila sails her yacht east across the International Date Line in the Pacific. Just before she crosses, the date is 1 April. What is the date just after?
b.why: Going east takes a day away, so the date goes back one day from 1 April. March has 31 days, so the day before 1 April is 31 March. 2 April comes from adding a day, which is what happens going west.
b.clue: Work out the direction rule first, then count one day.

problems.detail: 'The date is not changed by the distance travelled or the time of day' is confusing and, read literally, false: the date does change when the time passes midnight. It means the size of the change at the line is always one day, whatever the distance or time. Suggested rewording: 'The change is always one day, whatever the distance travelled or the time of day.'
